EmbodiedWorld-200K: Toward Embodied World Agents via Embodied-Planning Dataset and
Interactive World Models

Xiaokun Feng ††thanks: Equal contribution.    Junshu Tang11footnotemark: 1    Zeyi Lin    Ling-Hao Chen    Shuai Shao    Qinglin Lu    Kaiqi Huang    Tencent Hunyuan Affiliation: Project Page:https://xiaokunfeng.github.io/EmbodiedWorld-200K/
Abstract

Building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and act across diverse 3D worlds is a central research direction toward artificial general intelligence. Yet most existing work on embodied agents remains confined to specific tasks in a single scene and transfers poorly to new environments, leaving general embodied agents for open-world settings an important but under-explored direction. We refer to such agents as Embodied World Agents (EWAs), whose defining property is the ability to understand diverse visual environments and execute general actions in open-world conditions. To advance research on EWAs, we instantiate them on open-world embodied navigation-planning and release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale dataset of over 200K samples spanning diverse scenes. Each example is equipped with multi-level annotations, ranging from low-level camera-motion trajectories to high-level semantic instructions, and is accompanied by unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics, providing a shared substrate for offline pretraining and fair evaluation of EWAs. Beyond offline supervision, a defining characteristic of an EWA is its interaction with the environment; training solely on offline data is therefore insufficient, especially for generalizing to scenes not covered in the training distribution. Building dedicated real interactive environments, however, is often prohibitively expensive. To address this, we propose a novel training scheme that employs a video world model as a low-cost environment proxy and performs interactive reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training of the EWA within it. Empirically, pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K substantially improves the open-world embodied planning ability of the EWA, and further RL post-training inside a world model yields clear gains on out-of-distribution scenes. The full dataset, baseline checkpoints, and the accompanying training and evaluation code for supporting future research on EWAs are publicly available at https://xiaokunfeng.github.io/EmbodiedWorld-200K/.

1 Introduction

Vision–language large models (VLLMs) have demonstrated strong semantic understanding and multimodal reasoning capabilities [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. However, VLLMs are trained almost exclusively on static, passively observed data, rather than through executing actions or reasoning about their consequences in real environments; the intelligence they acquire thus remains, at its core, disembodied and passive [6, 7], and falls noticeably short on embodied tasks that require a closed perception–action loop [8, 9]. In response, building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and autonomously act in diverse 3D worlds [10, 11, 12] has attracted growing attention, and is widely regarded as one of the key paths toward artificial general intelligence.

Yet most existing work on embodied agents remains confined to specific tasks in a single scene—for example, navigation within a particular indoor simulator [13, 14], manipulation on a particular robotic platform [15, 10, 11, 16], or task execution within a single type of game [17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. By contrast, developing general-purpose embodied agents for broad open-world environments remains an important but under-explored direction. For ease of discussion, we refer to such agents as Embodied World Agents (EWAs): agents that aim to acquire both a general understanding of diverse visual environments in open worlds and a general ability to execute actions within them. While this vision is highly appealing, realizing it faces a fundamental infrastructure gap: the community currently lacks a large-scale, open-world dataset that can simultaneously support well-grounded training and unified evaluation, and a matching open-source baseline model together with a practical training recipe.

Existing embodied-agent datasets, such as typical Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) benchmarks [22, 14], are limited in scale, lack scene diversity, and offer only single-level annotations, preventing EWAs from learning robust, general-purpose priors through large-scale pretraining as VLLMs do. To fill this gap, we instantiate the EWA problem as open-world embodied navigation-planning, a task that jointly stresses perceiving a diverse visual scene, grounding a language goal within it, and executing an extended action sequence. We adopt this instantiation because translation and view rotation are the actions that remain universal across heterogeneous open worlds, and are also the action types that frontier video world models natively support [23, 24, 25]. Accordingly, we release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale public corpus for this task, comprising over 200K video clips collected from diverse open-world virtual game environments (as shown in Fig. 1). Each sample is accompanied by multi-level annotations, ranging from low-level camera-motion/action trajectories to high-level semantic instructions that describe the underlying embodied navigation-planning task. Building on this large-scale corpus of instruction–action sequences, we pretrain an existing VLLM [4] in an offline manner, retaining its multimodal understanding while extending it into a Vision–Language–Action (VLA) model [26, 10] with open-world embodied navigation-planning capabilities.

A defining property of EWAs is their interaction with open-world environments, where many required capabilities can only be acquired through closed-loop interaction. Consequently, training solely on EmbodiedWorld-200K in an offline manner is insufficient, particularly for generalization to unseen scenes. However, real-world interactive platforms, such as game engines, are limited in scalability across diverse environments. Fortunately, the rapid progress of video-generative world models (WMs) [27, 28, 29, 30, 24, 31, 32, 25] opens a new avenue: modern WMs can already roll out future visual observations conditioned on actions, offering a flexible and scalable simulation substrate for open-world interaction across diverse scenes. Building on this capability, we propose a novel training paradigm that treats a video WM as an environment proxy and performs interactive reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of EWAs within it. Specifically, an offline-pretrained EWA generates trajectories inside a frontier WM. During rollout, a VLLM dynamically produces task instructions conditioned on the evolving environment semantics, while reward signals are derived by framing reward modeling as visual question answering (QA) [33, 34]. Finally, we apply direct preference optimization (DPO) [35] on the collected trajectories, enabling the model to refine its policy from interactive feedback and improving embodied planning in unseen environments.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that offline pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K significantly improves the open-world embodied planning ability of EWAs, and that subsequent interactive RL post-training within a video world model further enhances adaptation to out-of-distribution (OOD) scenes. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We study general-purpose embodied agents for open-world environments, referred to as Embodied World Agents (EWAs), and position them as an important yet under-explored research direction. We further provide infrastructure support from both data and training perspectives.

  • •

    We release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale dataset for open-world embodied planning containing over 200K samples with multi-level annotations, together with a unified evaluation split and task-specific metrics, enabling standardized pretraining and fair evaluation of EWAs.

  • •

    We propose a two-stage training framework for EWAs and instantiate a corresponding baseline: offline pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K followed by interactive RL post-training using a video world model as a scalable environment proxy.

  • •

    Empirically, EmbodiedWorld-200K significantly improves embodied planning performance, while WM-based interactive post-training further enhances generalization to unseen scenes. We release the dataset, model weights, and code at the project page to support future research.

2 Related Work

Embodied agents.

Building agents that perceive and act in 3D environments has been studied across multiple domains. In robotic manipulation, RT-2 [12] finetunes a vision–language model to directly output robotic actions, PaLM-E [36] ingests multi-modal sensor streams into a large language model for embodied planning, SayCan [37] grounds language plans through learned affordances, and OpenVLA [10] and π0\pi_{0} [11] scale open-source vision–language–action (VLA) policies with large robot datasets such as Open X-Embodiment [15]. In embodied navigation, the community has long relied on photo-realistic simulators with curated trajectories [13, 14], yet these benchmarks remain limited to a few thousand paths in indoor scans. In open-world virtual environments, VPT [18] learns policies from unlabeled gameplay videos, MineDojo [17] provides Internet-scale knowledge for open-ended agents, Voyager [38] demonstrates LLM-driven lifelong exploration, STEVE-1 [19] trains a text-conditioned policy via latent goals, and SIMA [39] shows instruction-following across multiple 3D games. Despite this progress, most efforts remain confined to a single task type, scene distribution, or platform. The prospect of general-purpose embodied agents operating across diverse open worlds—what we term Embodied World Agents (EWAs)—remains largely unexplored, primarily due to the absence of large-scale, multi-level annotated data and a matching training recipe.

World (action) models.

World models learn environment dynamics to support agent training or planning. Classic model-based RL methods such as DreamerV3 [40] learn compact latent dynamics for policy optimization, while IRIS [41] builds autoregressive world models with transformers. Recent video-generative world models move toward pixel-level fidelity: Genie [23] learns controllable interactive environments from unlabeled video, GameNGen [42] and DIAMOND [43] simulate game engines with diffusion models, GAIA-1 [44] generates driving scenarios, and Cosmos [28] provides a large-scale foundation world model for physical AI. UniSim [45] further proposes learning interactive real-world simulators that unify visual, physical, and semantic signals. Connecting world models to downstream agents has been explored through several paradigms. Planning-based approaches use video generation as an imagination module for lookahead: Video Language Planning [46] leverages text-to-video models to synthesize visual plans, and RoboDreamer [47] composes world models for robot imagination. Data-augmentation methods generate synthetic trajectories for offline policy improvement, as in UniPi [48], which casts policy learning as text-guided video generation, and GenRL [49], which trains embodied policies inside a multimodal foundation world model. The paradigm closest to ours treats the world model as a closed-loop interactive environment for RL: UniSim [45] trains reward and policy jointly within a learned simulator, and GR-2 [50] uses generated video for a scalable robot post-training. However, these works predominantly target robotic manipulation with low-level motor commands, or operate on a single platform. Our work differs in both task scope and contribution form: we target embodied navigation and planning across general open-world scenes, and rather than proposing a new world model or RL algorithm, we provide reusable research infrastructure, a large-scale corpus (EmbodiedWorld-200K), a concrete task formulation, and a reproducible two-stage training recipe (offline pretraining + WM-based RL post-training). These efforts provide precisely the shared foundation left open by prior work.

3 The EmbodiedWorld-200K Dataset

We introduce EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale dataset for pretraining general-purpose embodied world agents across diverse open-world environments. Given that virtual 3D games have long served as a standard testbed for embodied-agent research [10, 11, 12], EmbodiedWorld-200K is assembled from 150 3D open-world games spanning a wide range of genres, yielding over 200K gameplay trajectories organized under a unified interaction format. Building on this corpus, we adopt open-world embodied navigation-planning as the central task for studying Embodied World Agents (EWAs), as it effectively stresses the ability of an agent to perceive, reason over, and act within diverse 3D environments. Targeted at this task, we apply a structured annotation process to the raw gameplay data. Specifically, each trajectory in EmbodiedWorld-200K is converted into a triplet consisting of an initial visual observation, a paired natural-language task instruction that specifies a diverse navigation-planning goal, and the expected action sequence the agent is supposed to execute in response. We detail the construction of EmbodiedWorld-200K in the following sections.

3.1 Data Collection

To support research on EWAs, the training corpus should cover a wide variety of 3D environments and enable the agent to perform a rich set of interactive tasks within them. However, few existing embodiment-related datasets meet both requirements simultaneously. Especially, datasets for robotic manipulation [51, 12, 52, 53, 54] focus on controlling a specific robot platform within relatively uniform environments, establishing VLN benchmarks [22, 14] are largely restricted to indoor scenes. Besides, autonomous-driving corpora [28, 55] are confined to the special case of road traffic. None of these can therefore be reused directly for our research. In contrast, virtual 3D games have long served as a natural proving ground for embodied-agent research [38, 56, 57, 20, 39, 7]. Modern 3D open-world games offer visually rich environments that obey physically plausible dynamics, and typically adopt first- or third-person viewpoints that align naturally with those of an embodied observer. More importantly, under a unified interaction logic, they jointly cover a broad spectrum of embodied behaviors such as navigation, exploration, and object interaction [58, 59], which makes them a highly suitable data platform for studying EWAs.

Motivated by this observation, we choose to build EmbodiedWorld-200K from gameplay data. Specifically, we adopt OGameData [60] as our data foundation: a publicly available, large-scale game-video repository that spans more than 150 next-generation 3D games and provides YouTube video URLs, temporal annotations, and structured captions for over one million gameplay clips, from which a multi-stage construction pipeline yields high-quality clips that are largely UI-free and strongly interaction-relevant. However, since OGameData was originally curated for open-world game video generation rather than for embodied-agent research, we further adapt it to the EWA setting through an additional filtering step. Concretely, we retain only clips that exhibit clear and continuous embodied actions, while discarding passive content such as cutscenes and menu navigation. To preserve genre-level diversity while staying aligned with the EWA task, we concentrate on open-world exploration, action-adventure, first-person shooter (FPS), puzzle-solving, and simulation games. After this process, we obtain 260K gameplay trajectories (∼\sim708 hours in total), which serve as the raw input to the annotation pipeline described in the next subsection.

3.2 Data Processing and Annotation Pipeline

The core contribution of EmbodiedWorld-200K lies in converting raw gameplay videos into structured agent training data via a dedicated annotation pipeline, illustrated in Fig. 2.

Task Formulation.

We instantiate the EWA study through the open-world embodied navigation-planning task, because it simultaneously stresses the three core abilities a general EWA must possess—perceiving a diverse visual environment, reasoning over the relation between goal and scene, and executing an extended action sequence within the world. Concretely, given a visual context in a 3D scene together with a natural-language goal instruction, the agent is required to produce the sequence of actions that fulfills this goal. Formally, an EWA carries out this task as

𝐚1:T=Agent(o0,ℓ),\mathbf{a}_{1:T}\;=\;\mathrm{Agent}\!\left(o_{0},\,\ell\right),

where o0o_{0} denotes the initial visual observation of episode, ℓ\ell is the natural-language task instruction describing a navigation-planning goal, and 𝐚1:T=(a1,a2,…,aT)\mathbf{a}_{1:T}=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{T}) is the expected action sequence to execute. Accordingly, each basic sample in the EWA task takes the form of a triplet (o0,ℓ,𝐚1:T)(o_{0},\,\ell,\,\mathbf{a}_{1:T}), and our annotation pipeline is organized around the construction of these three components.

As a preprocessing step, we first recover camera motion from each video clip using VIPE [61], to obtain 6-DoF pose trajectory capturing both translation and rotation. Together with raw gameplay videos, these camera trajectories form the input to the subsequent annotation pipeline (Fig. 2 (a)).

Step 1: Navigation-Coherent Segmentation and Extraction of o0o_{0}.

Although OGameData already provides scene-cut clips, they are not directly usable as EWA navigation units: within a single clip the subject’s motion can be visually incoherent, such as mixing drifting, backtracking, and frequent direction change. As a result, there is no single goal-directed trajectory whose intent we can attach an instruction to. Since navigation is naturally defined by a consistent principal motion direction towards some destination, we first segment each OGameData clip into shorter pieces that each carry one dominant motion direction. We refer to each such piece as a navigation-coherent segment (NCS), and adopt the NCS as the basic analysis unit throughout EmbodiedWorld-200K.

Concretely, starting from the camera pose sequence of a clip, we compute a smoothed per-frame displacement, track the cumulative principal motion direction, and trigger a cut whenever the instantaneous motion deviates from this principal direction by more than a preset angle for several consecutive frames. After further discarding erratic and overly short candidates, we obtain in total 215K NCSs from the raw gameplay clips. Each surviving NCS carries a well-defined principal motion direction, i.e., a clear navigation intent. Therefore, we directly take its initial frame as the visual observation o0o_{0} of the corresponding EWA sample. The exact thresholds and full implementation details of this procedure are deferred to App. A.1.

Step 2: Discrete Action Quantization and Derivation of 𝐚1:T\mathbf{a}_{1:T}.

For every NCS, we derive the agent action sequence 𝐚1:T\mathbf{a}_{1:T} by discretizing the camera-pose motion into a unified W/A/S/D action space shared across all games:

  • •

    Translation: W (forward), A (left), S (backward), D (right), N (stationary)

  • •

    Rotation: W (pitch up), A (yaw left), S (pitch down), D (yaw right), N (no rotation)

The central design question is how to calibrate the physical amount of motion that each translation/rotation token should represent. This calibration directly controls the distribution of TT across NCSs: too coarse a unit yields sequences that are too short to carry fine-grained navigation signals, whereas too fine a unit produces sequences that are too long to learn efficiently. Therefore, we initially run a dataset-wide statistic on the per-NCS motion magnitude, and pick a translation unit and a rotation unit from this distribution that make the resulting TT lie in a sensible range. With these two units fixed, we scan each NCS in temporal order and emit a new W/A/S/D token whenever the accumulated motion reaches one unit, independently for translation and rotation, so that the two streams remain aligned. As a result, every NCS is converted into a variable-length W/A/S/D sequence in which each token corresponds to an approximately fixed amount of physical motion. Detailed statistics, the exact discretization procedure, and additional robustness safeguards are provided in App. A.2.

Step 3: Annotation of the Navigation Task Instruction ℓ\ell.

Given the initial visual observation o0o_{0} and the direction-coherent action sequence 𝐚1:T\mathbf{a}_{1:T}, the remaining component of the triplet, the natural-language task instruction ℓ\ell, is obtained by automatic prompting of a frontier vision-language model, Qwen3.5-27B [4]. For each NCS we feed into the VLLM a set of frames uniformly sampled from the corresponding video segment, together with an overall direction descriptor derived from 𝐚1:T\mathbf{a}_{1:T}, and prompt the model to produce a natural-language instruction that summarizes the embodied-navigation task implicitly carried by that segment. To accommodate different annotation granularities, we design two complementary instruction types:

  • •

    Detailed Movement Instruction. A fine-grained description of how the agent should move throughout the segment, combining direction cues with the visible target—e.g., “The character advances forward along a narrow dirt path, heading toward the line of trees visible directly ahead.”

  • •

    High-Level Goal-Navigation Instruction. A direction-agnostic description that specifies only the destination to reach, with no movement cue attached, e.g., “Head to the line of trees.” or “Navigate to the wooden gate structure.” Compared with the detailed instruction above, this higher-level variant is noticeably more challenging. Moreover, it is not always producible, because it requires the navigation target to be uniquely identifiable within the segment. Therefore, we design an automatic grounding–verification procedure admitting only the NCSs satisfying this condition into this type of annotation.

When constructing the final training data, for each NCS we adopt a higher-level-first, detailed-fallback policy: we use the goal-navigation caption as ℓ\ell whenever it is successfully produced, and otherwise fall back to the detailed movement instruction. Fig. 6 (a) and (b) present representative examples of the Detailed Movement Instruction and the High-Level Goal-Navigation Instruction, respectively, and more examples can be found in Fig. 1. The full prompts, the grounding–verification procedure, and the post-hoc consistency-check rules are deferred to App. A.3.

3.3 Statistical Analysis

Based on the NCSs extracted above, we carry out a statistical analysis around the core triplet (o0,ℓ,𝐚1:T)(o_{0},\,\ell,\,\mathbf{a}_{1:T}), to offer a direct view of how well EmbodiedWorld-200K matches the needs of EWA research. Firstly, the visual observation o0o_{0} reflects the type of world each sample is drawn from, and is thus the most direct lens for evaluating environmental diversity. Fig. 3 (a) shows a word cloud over the descriptive keywords of the observed environments, and Fig. 3 (b–c) provide finer-grained breakdowns along the game-genre and scene-category axes. Complementary per-dimension statistics (camera viewpoint, art style, etc.) are reported in Fig. A1. Overall, these plots indicate that EmbodiedWorld-200K spans a wide variety of 3D environments rather than being dominated by any single scene type.

Besides, the action sequence 𝐚1:T\mathbf{a}_{1:T} captures the granularity and length of the operations the agent is expected to execute. Fig. 5 (a) plots the distribution of sequence lengths TT, while Fig. 5 (b) shows a heatmap of per-position token occurrences across all NCSs. The fraction of samples decreases as TT grows, which is consistent with our design choice that the navigation target typically appears in the initial frame o0o_{0}. That is to say, the agent–target distance therefore stays moderate and does not call for excessively long sequences. The mean length of 9.98 serves as an appropriate operating point, covering both short-range fine adjustments and longer-range continuous progressions. Finally, for the task instruction ℓ\ell, we primarily examine whether the set of navigation goals is sufficiently rich. Fig. 5 shows a word cloud over the target-location phrases extracted from ℓ\ell, confirming that the covered goals span a wide variety of object and place categories. The above analyses collectively demonstrate that EmbodiedWorld-200K provides rich diversity and broad coverage across its three core components (visual environments, action sequences, and task instructions), offering a solid data foundation on which EWA research can be built.

3.4 Evaluation Metrics

We partition the curated NCSs into disjoint training and evaluation splits so that all methods are trained and benchmarked under a unified protocol [62]. Our metrics are designed to quantitatively assess instruction-conditioned trajectory following and goal arrival [63]. Drawing on standard practice in Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) and tailored to our discrete W/A/S/D action format, we report four complementary metrics that span token-level and trajectory-level performance (see App. B for algorithmic details):

  • •

    TM (Token Match, ↑\uparrow): mean per-step keyset-F1 between predicted and ground-truth tokens, computed separately on the translation and rotation streams and then averaged.

  • •

    DirAcc (Direction Accuracy, ↑\uparrow): global-direction accuracy averaged over four axes (translation forward/backward and left/right, rotation pitch and yaw).

  • •

    nDTW (normalized Dynamic Time Warping, ↑\uparrow): normalized DTW over reconstructed 3D trajectories, averaged over a distance-tolerance coefficient τ∈{0.5,1.0,2.0}\tau\in\{0.5,1.0,2.0\} that controls how strictly per-step deviations are penalized.

  • •

    NE (Navigation Error, ↓\downarrow): terminal xy displacement measured in translation units.

4 EWA Baseline Method

To facilitate future research on EWAs, we present a simple baseline that turns a frontier VLLM into an EWA through a dedicated two-stage training scheme. Concretely, we conduct large-scale offline pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K, and then perform interactive RL post-training with a video world model acting as environmental proxy. We describe each component as follows.

4.1 Model Architecture

Although frontier VLLMs have demonstrated strong multimodal understanding, the intelligence they acquire remains essentially disembodied: they observe passively and lack a native mechanism for producing physical actions in the environment [7]. Our baseline therefore takes a frontier VLLM (i.e., Qwen-VL [4]) as backbone and extends it into a VLA model for open-world embodied planning. We deliberately refrain from introducing heavyweight extra components such as dedicated action heads [64, 11, 65], and instead keep both the task instruction and the predicted action sequence entirely within VLLM native text-token space. This minimally intrusive design preserves the understanding capability inherited from VLLM pretraining while providing a simple, easy-to-extend baseline for follow-up work. Concretely, the visual observation o0o_{0} and the task instruction ℓ\ell are concatenated through a dedicated system prompt as input, and the model is asked to emit the full action sequence 𝐚1:T\mathbf{a}_{1:T} as a single JSON object. Detailed prompt is provided in App C.

4.2 Two-Stage Training

To equip VLLM with open-world embodied-planning ability, we first perform offline pretraining on our EmbodiedWorld-200K dataset so that the model can absorb the open-world embodied-planning priors latent in this large-scale corpus. Building on this offline-pretrained EWA, we further introduce a second stage of interactive RL post-training. This stage targets adaptation to specific environments, especially scenes outside the training distribution, where closed-loop interaction is crucial. To make such interaction scalable, we use a video world model [25] as a low-cost environment proxy.

Stage I: Offline supervised pretraining.

We finetune Qwen3-VL-4B [4] on the training split of EmbodiedWorld-200K with a cross-entropy loss between the predicted and ground-truth action tokens. This stage injects broad open-world embodied-planning priors — drawn from a diverse distribution of scenes and instructions — into the model.

Stage II: Interactive RL post-training inside a video world model.

Stage I is purely offline, and its coverage is therefore bounded by the training distribution. To further adapt the baseline to a particular target environment, especially one outside the coverage of EmbodiedWorld-200K, closed-loop interaction is necessary. Since building real interactive platforms at open-world scale is prohibitively expensive, we instead leverage a frontier video world model [25, 27, 29, 66] as a low-cost environment proxy. The Stage-I baseline is rolled out inside this proxy environment, and the resulting trajectories are used for RL post-training. Although conceptually straightforward, realising this pipeline requires careful design at every step. The core recipe of our scheme is as follows: for each rollout, a VLLM is conditioned on the current scene to adaptively generate a natural-language task instruction ℓ\ell, which in turn anchors a visual question-answering (VQA) reward that judges whether the rollout fulfils the instruction; the resulting preference trajectory pairs are then consumed by Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) [35, 67] to further post-train the baseline. In this way, we aim to substantially enhance the baseline’s embodied-planning ability in specific target scenes without requiring any additional human annotation. Further implementation details are provided in App. D.

5 Experimental Results and Discussion

Based on the two training stages introduced above, we report key implementation details and present the main empirical findings.

5.1 EmbodiedWorld-200K pretraining substantially boosts embodied navigation-planning

We finetune Qwen3-VL-4B [4] with LoRA on the training split of EmbodiedWorld-200K for 2 epochs. To position the resulting model rather than only measure our own improvement, we further evaluate three families of external baselines on the same evaluation split, with the same metric toolkit and the same prompt. (a) VLN models. Uni-NaVid [68] and StreamVLN [69] are recent vision-and-language navigation policies; we map their native action vocabularies onto our W/A/S/D format one step per token. (b) A game foundation model. NitroGen [70] predicts gamepad actions from pixels after large-scale gameplay pretraining; since it is not language-conditioned, it serves as an instruction-free lower bound that isolates how much of the task is solvable from visual reaction alone. (c) Zero-shot frontier VLMs. The open-source InternVL3-8B [71] and the proprietary Gemini-3.5 are prompted with our baseline system prompt without any finetuning. The last two rows of Tab. 1 are our own backbone, Qwen3-VL-4B, before and after Stage-I pretraining.

Three observations follow. First, Stage-I SFT improves every metric over the zero-shot backbone (TM +7.1+7.1, DirAcc +1.9+1.9, nDTW +16.5+16.5, NE −16.1-16.1), confirming that the corpus injects the intended open-world navigation-planning priors. Second, these gains are not obtainable from a stronger general-purpose model: our model leads every external baseline on TM, nDTW and NE (+9.2+9.2, +20.2+20.2 and −19.1-19.1 over the strongest competitor) and matches the best DirAcc (72.072.0 vs. 72.472.4); notably, Gemini-3.5 attains that best DirAcc yet trails markedly on the trajectory-level metrics, indicating that strong multimodal understanding suffices to infer the coarse heading but not to reproduce the goal-directed action sequence itself. Third, the benchmark is discriminative rather than saturated: baseline scores span a wide range (TM 45.345.3–54.954.9, nDTW 25.925.9–67.167.1, NE 51.751.7–114.7114.7), and the instruction-free NitroGen records the lowest DirAcc (39.839.8, close to chance), confirming that the task genuinely requires grounding the language instruction rather than reacting to pixels alone.

In addition, Fig. 6 shows qualitative examples on evaluation split, and Fig. 7 further shows out-of-distribution samples whose initial observations o0o_{0} are synthesized by an image-generation model [72]. We further analyze the effect of the Stage-I pretraining data scale in App. C.1. In summary, results show that pretraining on the proposed dataset successfully injects expected open-world embodied-planning priors for model.

5.2 World-model-based RL post-training improves target-scene adaptation

Stage I essentially fits the model to a broad collection of world environments and extracts the common knowledge shared across them; its capacity is therefore inherently bounded by the training distribution. To further adapt the model to a particular target environment — for example, to calibrate the precise physical magnitude that each unit action corresponds to under that environment’s dynamics — closed-loop interaction with, and post-training on, that very environment is indispensable. This mirrors the common recipe in embodied-robotics research [10, 11, 12], where a model is first pretrained on broad and diverse corpora and then finetuned on a specific robot platform to adapt to its physical characteristics. Since directly building a real interactive platform is prohibitively expensive, we instead resort to a frontier video world model [25] as a low-cost proxy. Concretely, we use LingBot-World-Fast [25] as the interactive proxy and take GTA5 as an illustrative target environment. GTA5 is an open-world game widely used in academic research [73, 74], yet it is not included in our training distribution. We therefore treat it as a representative setting in which large-scale sampling of real trajectories is costly.

Fig. 8 gives an overview of the resulting Stage-II pipeline: an initial observation and an automatically generated task instruction are fed to the actor, which samples a candidate action sequence; the sequence is executed inside the video world model to obtain the corresponding rollout frames, on which a VQA reward judges how well the instruction is fulfilled and yields a preferred/rejected action pair for DPO. We outline the key design choices below and defer the full implementation to App. D. Within this proxy, we align the physical magnitude that each unit control action produces in the GTA5 environment with that produced inside LingBot-World-Fast [25], and then initialize the actor with the Stage-I SFT model rather than the base VLLM. We adopt the SFT model as the actor because it has a basic embodied-planning ability, so that its action sequences contain a non-trivial fraction of correct decisions; combined with exploration, this yields rollouts of sufficient quality to form informative preference pairs for DPO [75]. Starting from the base model would produce rollouts too noisy to support effective preference learning. We therefore roll out the SFT actor inside LingBot-World-Fast [25], construct preference pairs from the collected trajectories, and perform DPO post-training on the actor. Tab. 2 reports results on our GTA5-specific evaluation split curated from the game. DPO post-training on top of the Stage-I baseline significantly improves target-scene adaptation.

6 Conclusion

In this work, we identified Embodied World Agents (EWAs)—general-purpose embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and act across diverse open-world 3D environments—as an important yet under-explored research direction, and contributed infrastructure support from both the data and training perspectives. On the data side, we released EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale open-world embodied-planning corpus of over 200K samples with multi-level annotations ranging from low-level camera-motion trajectories to high-level semantic instructions, together with a unified evaluation split and four task-specific metrics for fair and reproducible comparison. On the training side, we proposed a two-stage training framework and instantiated a concrete baseline: offline supervised pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K followed by interactive RL post-training that leverages a frontier video world model as a low-cost environment proxy. Empirically, offline pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K substantially strengthens open-world embodied planning ability across all four evaluation metrics, while world-model-based interactive post-training further improves adaptation to out-of-distribution scenes. We release the dataset, checkpoints, and code as a shared foundation for EWA research.

Appendix A More Details About the EmbodiedWorld-200K Construction Pipeline

This appendix complements Sec. 3.2 and provides the full specification of the three annotation steps that turn a raw gameplay clip into a triplet (o0,ℓ,𝐚1:T)(o_{0},\ell,\mathbf{a}_{1:T}): (i) navigation-coherent segmentation, (ii) magnitude-based variable-length W/A/S/D discretization, and (iii) instruction annotation with verification.

A.1 Navigation-Coherent Segmentation

We start from the 6-DoF camera trajectory recovered by VIPE [61]. For each clip, we first re-express the per-frame poses in a local coordinate frame anchored at the first frame and smooth the resulting signal with a sliding-window average of size Wsmooth=5W_{\text{smooth}}=5 to suppress high-frequency jitter.

Principal-direction tracking and cut criterion.

On the smoothed signal we maintain a running estimate of the cumulative principal motion direction. Whenever the instantaneous motion deviates from this principal direction by more than θcut=90∘\theta_{\text{cut}}=90^{\circ} for at least Fcut=3F_{\text{cut}}=3 consecutive frames, a cut is triggered; the portion between two adjacent cuts is treated as one candidate navigation-coherent segment (NCS). Intuitively, this criterion ensures that every NCS corresponds to a temporally continuous interval during which the agent moves towards a stable destination.

Quality filters.

The coarse segmentation above is followed by two filters to discard erratic or under-informative candidates:

  • •

    Displacement-vs-path-length ratio. For each candidate segment we compute the ratio of its net displacement (start-to-end straight-line distance) to the integrated path length. Candidates with a ratio below ρdisp=0.3\rho_{\text{disp}}=0.3, or whose curvature variance exceeds σκ2=1.5\sigma_{\kappa}^{2}=1.5, are dropped as overly meandering or shaky.

  • •

    Minimum-length constraint. Any remaining candidate shorter than Lmin=60L_{\text{min}}=60 frames is dropped, so that each surviving NCS contains enough visual context for the downstream annotation model to reason about the navigation goal.

Initial observation o0o_{0} and frame-index alignment.

The first frame of every surviving NCS is exported as the initial visual observation o0o_{0} of the corresponding EWA sample. When the recovered-pose sampling rate disagrees with the video sampling rate, we remap the pose-index of the first frame to the corresponding video-index before exporting, so that o0o_{0} is strictly aligned with the first pose used by the NCS.

A.2 Magnitude-Based Variable-Length W/A/S/D Discretization

As stated in Sec. 3.2 Step 2, the central design question here is how to calibrate the physical amount of motion that each W/A/S/D token represents: too coarse a unit yields too-short sequences that cannot carry fine-grained navigation signals, whereas too fine a unit produces overly long sequences that are hard to learn. Our magnitude-based variable-length discretization procedure is organized around this calibration.

Unit calibration from dataset-level statistics.

For each NCS we compute its total translation Ltrans=∑i∥𝐩i+1−𝐩i∥L_{\text{trans}}=\sum_{i}\lVert\mathbf{p}_{i+1}-\mathbf{p}_{i}\rVert (integrated path length) and total rotation Lrot=∑iΔ​yawi2+Δ​pitchi2L_{\text{rot}}=\sum_{i}\sqrt{\Delta\text{yaw}_{i}^{2}+\Delta\text{pitch}_{i}^{2}} (in degrees). We then sweep candidate values of the translation unit Δtrans\Delta_{\text{trans}} and inspect, for each candidate, the induced distribution of sequence length TT across the entire corpus; the smallest unit for which TT lies in a training-friendly range is retained. The rotation unit Δrot\Delta_{\text{rot}} has a natural absolute scale and is fixed throughout. Our final release adopts

Δtrans=0.05,Δrot=5∘.\Delta_{\text{trans}}=0.05,\qquad\Delta_{\text{rot}}=5^{\circ}.

Mixed-motion accumulator and bin boundaries.

With Δtrans\Delta_{\text{trans}} and Δrot\Delta_{\text{rot}} fixed, we scan an NCS in temporal order and track a single scalar budget

mi=∥𝐩i+1−𝐩i∥Δtrans+Δ​yawi2+Δ​pitchi2Δrot.m_{i}=\frac{\lVert\mathbf{p}_{i+1}-\mathbf{p}_{i}\rVert}{\Delta_{\text{trans}}}\,+\,\frac{\sqrt{\Delta\text{yaw}_{i}^{2}+\Delta\text{pitch}_{i}^{2}}}{\Delta_{\text{rot}}}.

The budget is accumulated frame by frame and a new bin is closed whenever the running sum reaches 1.01.0; any residual below 1.01.0 at the end of the segment is merged into the last bin. This yields a time-synchronous partitioning of the NCS in which every bin corresponds to an approximately unit-magnitude motion, jointly measured in translation and rotation.

Per-bin W/A/S/D token.

Within each bin we emit one translation token and one rotation token by evaluating the net displacement (Δ​x,Δ​y)(\Delta x,\Delta y) and the net rotation (Δ​yaw,Δ​pitch)(\Delta\text{yaw},\Delta\text{pitch}) accumulated inside the bin. For either stream, the principal axis is first identified by the larger absolute magnitude and, if the secondary axis exceeds the principal axis by a ratio of 0.30.3 (translation) or 0.50.5 (rotation), the two keys are combined into a diagonal token such as WD. To suppress jitter, we additionally reject a bin-level token as N when (i) its total magnitude is below 10%10\% of the corresponding unit, or (ii) the net-to-accumulated ratio is below 0.40.4, a condition characteristic of back-and-forth oscillation. A whole NCS whose total translation and rotation both stay below static thresholds (0.020.02 in pose units and 2.5∘2.5^{\circ}) collapses to a single N token on each stream.

Output.

The procedure produces two equally long W/A/S/D sequences—one for translation and one for rotation—in which each token carries an approximately fixed physical meaning of ∼0.05{\sim}0.05 in translation or ∼5∘{\sim}5^{\circ} in rotation. These two streams are stored together with their segment-level metadata (e.g., LtransL_{\text{trans}}, LrotL_{\text{rot}}, bin boundaries) alongside the raw annotation JSON and are used as the ground-truth action sequence 𝐚1:T\mathbf{a}_{1:T} throughout this work.

A.3 Instruction Annotation and Verification

This subsection details how the natural-language task instruction ℓ\ell is produced for each NCS. Following the two-track design in Sec. 3.2 Step 3, we generate two complementary annotations per NCS—a Detailed Movement Instruction and, whenever feasible, a High-Level Goal-Navigation Caption—and adopt a higher-level-first, detailed-fallback policy when assembling the final training corpus. Both tracks are implemented via automatic prompting of the same frontier VLLM, Qwen3.5-27B [4], served with vLLM tensor parallelism.

Detailed Movement Instruction.

For each NCS we uniformly sample frames from the corresponding video segment at 22 fps and feed them, together with an overall direction descriptor derived from 𝐚1:T\mathbf{a}_{1:T} (e.g., "left-forward"), into the VLLM under the prompt shown below. The VLLM is asked to emit a structured JSON record with four fields—annotatable, task_description, move_target, and move_type—together with a self-reported direction_consist flag indicating whether the described motion is consistent with the direction descriptor.

Post-hoc direction-consistency check.

To catch annotations that silently contradict the underlying action sequence, every record produced above is re-evaluated by an independent call that parses both the direction descriptor and the free-text move_type into a pair of axis-level labels (forward/backward and left/right) and compares them. Any NCS whose two labels disagree on either axis is removed from the Detailed Movement Instruction pool.

High-Level Goal-Navigation Caption.

The higher-level variant specifies only the navigation destination without any directional cues. Because it requires the target to be uniquely identifiable within the NCS, we produce it through a four-step grounding-and-verification loop:

  1. 1.

    strip direction words from the move_target field of the Detailed Movement Instruction to obtain a candidate target phrase;

  2. 2.

    ground the candidate phrase on the initial observation o0o_{0} with an open-vocabulary detector, keeping only cases in which exactly one bounding box is returned;

  3. 3.

    ground the same phrase on the final frame of the NCS, again keeping only single-bbox cases;

  4. 4.

    perform an LLM-based same-entity verification between the two boxes.

Only NCSs that pass all four checks are admitted to this track, and the VLLM is prompted to generate a short, direction-free goal-navigation caption conditioned on the verified target phrase (e.g., “Head to the line of trees.” or “Navigate to the wooden gate structure.”).

Training-data construction policy.

When assembling the final training corpus, we adopt a higher-level-first, detailed-fallback policy: we use the Goal-Navigation Caption as ℓ\ell whenever it is successfully produced, and otherwise fall back to the Detailed Movement Instruction. The NCS-level share of each track in the released dataset is reported in Fig. 3 and the accompanying statistics.

What the segment endpoint certifies.

Because every trajectory-level metric is anchored at the endpoint of the ground-truth NCS, it is worth stating precisely what that endpoint does and does not guarantee. The segmentation itself is triggered by a change of principal motion direction (App. A.1) rather than by a verified arrival, so an NCS endpoint is not, on its own, a certificate that the agent reached a target object. The goal–endpoint correspondence is instead established by the annotation procedure above: an NCS is admitted to the High-Level Goal-Navigation track only if a target object is identifiable in its final frame and survives all four grounding-and-verification checks, so that for this track the endpoint is, by construction, a position at which the instructed target has been reached. For the Detailed Movement Instruction track no such claim is made: the instruction describes the movement that the segment carries out, and the endpoint is simply where that movement ends. The metrics are defined to respect this distinction—they score the displacement consistency between the predicted and ground-truth endpoints rather than physical contact with an object—as discussed in App. B.3.

A.4 Additional Statistical Analyses

This subsection complements Sec. 3.3, in which the diversity of the visual observation o0o_{0} is analyzed through a keyword word cloud together with two coarse-grained breakdowns along the game-genre and scene-category axes (Fig. 3). To provide a more comprehensive view of environment diversity, we further report per-dimension distributions of o0o_{0} along additional metadata axes, including camera viewpoint, art style, and other auxiliary attributes, as summarized in Fig. A1. These plots reinforce the conclusion drawn in the main text: EmbodiedWorld-200K spans a broad and well-balanced distribution of 3D environments along every examined axis, providing a solid visual foundation on which EWAs can acquire open-world priors through offline pretraining.

Appendix B More Details About Evaluation Metrics

This appendix complements Sec. 3.4 and specifies the full algorithmic details of the four evaluation metrics. Following the organization in the main paper, we first describe the two token-level metrics — TM and DirAcc — that assess the predicted action sequence on a per-step basis, and then describe the two trajectory-level metrics — nDTW and NE — that evaluate the reconstructed 3-D trajectory as a whole. We also specify the shared pre-processing rules (length alignment and parse-failure fallback) that apply to all four metrics.

Shared pre-processing.

For every evaluation sample we parse the predicted and ground-truth action sequences into translation and rotation token lists. Before computing any token-level metric, both sequences are right-padded with the no-op token N to a common length L=max⁡(|𝐚^|,|𝐚|)L=\max(|\hat{\mathbf{a}}|,|\mathbf{a}|), so that length mismatches are penalized symmetrically. A sample whose prediction fails JSON parsing is replaced by a single-token no-op [N][\texttt{N}] on each stream and scored through the identical pipeline, so that no samples are dropped from the evaluation pool.

B.1 Token-level metrics

TM (Token Match, ↑\uparrow).

TM measures how well the predicted keys at each time step match the ground-truth keys, and is robust to the fact that a combined token such as WD only partially overlaps with a simpler token such as W. Concretely, we treat each token as a subset of {W,A,S,D}\{\texttt{W},\texttt{A},\texttt{S},\texttt{D}\}, with N identified with ∅\varnothing. Let gtg_{t} and ptp_{t} denote the ground-truth and predicted token sets at step tt; we compute a per-step set-level F1F_{1},

Pt=|gt∩pt||pt|,Rt=|gt∩pt||gt|,F1(t)=2​Pt​RtPt+Rt,P_{t}=\frac{|g_{t}\cap p_{t}|}{|p_{t}|},\quad R_{t}=\frac{|g_{t}\cap p_{t}|}{|g_{t}|},\quad F_{1}^{(t)}=\frac{2\,P_{t}\,R_{t}}{P_{t}+R_{t}},

with the convention that F1(t):=1F_{1}^{(t)}:=1 when gt=pt=∅g_{t}=p_{t}=\varnothing and F1(t):=0F_{1}^{(t)}:=0 when exactly one side is empty. TM is obtained by averaging F1(t)F_{1}^{(t)} over all LL steps on each stream, and then averaging the translation and rotation scores.

DirAcc (Direction Accuracy, ↑\uparrow).

DirAcc probes whether the overall direction of motion is captured correctly on four independent axes: translation forward/backward, translation left/right, rotation pitch, and rotation yaw. For each axis we derive a single categorical label in {positive,negative,neutral}\{\text{positive},\text{negative},\text{neutral}\} by comparing the counts of the two opposing keys across the full sequence (e.g., count of W versus count of S on the translation FB axis). DirAcc is the mean four-axis agreement between the predicted labels and the ground-truth labels over the evaluation set.

B.2 Trajectory-level metrics

Trajectory reconstruction.

All trajectory-level metrics are computed on 3-D trajectories reconstructed from the discrete W/A/S/D sequences with the dataset-calibrated physical units of Δtrans=0.05\Delta_{\text{trans}}=0.05 and Δrot=5∘\Delta_{\text{rot}}=5^{\circ}. Starting from the origin (x,y,z,yaw,pitch)=𝟎(x,y,z,\text{yaw},\text{pitch})=\mathbf{0}, at each step we first apply the rotation token to update the heading, and then apply the translation token in the body-frame forward direction; composite tokens (e.g., WD) contribute to both of their component axes. This yields a pose sequence of length |𝐚|+1|\mathbf{a}|{+}1 for both the prediction and the ground truth.

nDTW (normalized Dynamic Time Warping, ↑\uparrow).

nDTW assesses path shape while absorbing moderate misalignments in pace between the two trajectories. Standard dynamic time warping on the reconstructed 3-D point sequences yields a cumulative distance DTW⁡(𝐚^,𝐚)\mathrm{DTW}(\hat{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{a}), which we normalize by the ground-truth length and a distance-tolerance coefficient τ\tau,

nDTW⁡(τ)=exp⁡(−DTW⁡(𝐚^,𝐚)|𝐚|⋅τ).\mathrm{nDTW}(\tau)\;=\;\exp\!\left(-\,\frac{\mathrm{DTW}(\hat{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{a})}{|\mathbf{a}|\cdot\tau}\right).

We report nDTW=𝔼τ∈{0.5,1.0,2.0}​nDTW​(τ)\mathrm{nDTW}=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\in\{0.5,1.0,2.0\}}\mathrm{nDTW}(\tau) to cover strict, moderate, and loose deviation tolerances.

NE (Navigation Error, ↓\downarrow).

NE directly reports the planar endpoint displacement NE=dx​y\mathrm{NE}=d_{xy} in translation units, where dx​yd_{xy} denotes the planar distance between the predicted and the ground-truth endpoint. Complementary to the shape-based nDTW, it provides a threshold-free, purely endpoint-based readout of whether the agent reproduces the goal-directed displacement described by the instruction.

B.3 What the Metrics Do and Do Not Measure

The two trajectory-level metrics are deliberately complementary, and reading them together is what makes the evaluation well-posed. We make their division of labour, and its two main consequences, explicit here.

Path shape versus goal displacement.

nDTW is a path-shape measure: it rewards following the reference trajectory and therefore penalizes an alternative route that reaches the same destination by a different path. NE is path-agnostic: it compares only the two endpoints, so any route that arrives at the same displacement receives the same score. Because we report both, the two orthogonal questions—“did the agent arrive where the instruction asked?” (NE) and “did it follow the reference path?” (nDTW)—are read out independently, and neither can silently dominate the other. In particular, nDTW’s penalty on valid alternative paths does not drive any conclusion in this paper: every headline comparison is accompanied by NE, which does not share that penalty. The converse also holds, which is why we do not report NE alone: an agent that reaches the right endpoint through an erratic detour is distinguishable only through nDTW.

Displacement consistency, not physical contact.

As noted in App. A.3, the endpoint of an NCS marks the end of a direction-coherent movement, and only for the High-Level Goal-Navigation track is it additionally verified to be a position at which an identifiable target has been reached. Our endpoint metric is defined to match this weaker guarantee: NE measures whether the agent reproduces the overall goal-directed displacement that the instruction describes, not whether it physically touches the target object. It is therefore insensitive to the precise contact geometry at the goal, and robust to the residual localization error of the monocular pose reconstruction from which the ground truth is derived.

Capabilities outside the scope of these metrics.

All four metrics score an instruction-conditioned action sequence against a reference sequence. They consequently do not evaluate object interaction or manipulation, recovery from execution errors, long-horizon task decomposition, or any behaviour that changes the state of the environment; nor do they capture exploration under partial observability, since the instruction and the initial observation are given. We regard these as complementary axes left to future benchmarks (App. E), and the numbers reported here should be read as evidence about open-world navigation-planning specifically.

Appendix C More Details About Stage I: Pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K

This appendix complements Sec. 4 and Sec. 5.1 by providing the full implementation details of Stage I.

Training recipe and compute.

We instantiate the baseline with Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct [4] and perform LoRA [76] fine-tuning on the training split of EmbodiedWorld-200K. The LoRA adapters are attached to all linear layers of the backbone with rank r=32r=32, scaling factor α=64\alpha=64, and dropout 0.0050.005. Each training sample pairs an initial observation o0o_{0} with the instruction ℓ\ell and the ground-truth action sequence 𝐚1:T\mathbf{a}_{1:T}; the image pixel budget is capped between 12,54412{,}544 and 451,584451{,}584 pixels and the sequence length is capped at 4,0964{,}096 tokens. We use AdamW with learning rate 1​e−41\mathrm{e}{-4}, a cosine schedule with 5%5\% linear warm-up, weight decay 0.010.01, and bf16 mixed precision with DeepSpeed ZeRO-3. The effective batch size is 256256 (per-device batch size 8×8\times gradient-accumulation steps 4×84\times 8 GPUs), and we train for two epochs. The full Stage I run is carried out on 8×8\times NVIDIA H20 GPUs with a wall-clock time of approximately 55 hours (∼40\sim\!40 GPU-hours in total).

Baseline system prompt.

At inference time, the baseline receives (o0,ℓ)(o_{0},\ell) through a fixed system prompt that specifies the task, the discrete W/A/S/D action space, the physical meaning of each unit token, and the required JSON output format. The same prompt is used throughout training and evaluation, and is reproduced verbatim below.

C.1 Effect of the Stage-I Pretraining Data Scale

To understand how much of EmbodiedWorld-200K is actually needed to drive the Stage-I gains reported in Sec. 5.1, we additionally ablate the training-set size by pretraining the baseline on {1/3,2/3,3/3}\{1/3,2/3,3/3\} uniformly sub-sampled shards of the full training split while keeping the remaining training recipe and the held-out evaluation split exactly the same as in App. C.

As shown in Tab. A1, every metric improves substantially over the zero-shot Base model at every data scale, confirming that the Stage-I gains are driven by the scale of EmbodiedWorld-200K rather than by any specific subset. A closer look at the per-metric gains reveals two distinct regimes: the trajectory-level metrics (nDTW and NE) already capture most of their improvement with only one-third of the corpus (nDTW →83.067.1\!\to\!83.0, NE →40.151.7\!\to\!40.1) and then plateau, while TM keeps growing steadily across all data scales (→→→62.054.9\!\to\!56.3\!\to\!59.7\!\to\!62.0); DirAcc, which only probes the overall direction on each axis, is largely saturated already at the backbone level and stays flat throughout. In other words, the macroscopic navigation structure of open-world 3D scenes—when to turn, how far to travel, and where to arrive—is relatively data-efficient on top of a strong VLLM prior, whereas fine-grained per-step precision continues to benefit from additional data; both observations are consistent with the view that EmbodiedWorld-200K provides the scale and diversity needed to elicit open-world embodied navigation-planning priors from a frontier VLLM.

Appendix D More Details About Stage II: World-Model-Based RL Post-Training

This appendix complements Sec. 4 and Sec. 5.2 and provides the full implementation details of Stage II. As stated in the main text, Stage II treats a frontier video world model (LingBot-World-Fast [25]) as a low-cost proxy for the target environment (GTA5), and post-trains the Stage-I actor with DPO [35] on preference pairs collected via closed-loop rollouts. Turning this conceptually simple recipe into a reproducible pipeline, however, requires careful design at every step. We organise the implementation into four tightly coupled stages—(i) initial observation and candidate action collection in the real game environment, (ii) rollout inside the world model, (iii) VQA-based reward scoring and preference-pair construction, and (iv) DPO optimisation—and describe each below.

Step 1: Initial observation and candidate action collection.

We use the real GTA5 environment solely to (a) harvest diverse initial observations o0o_{0} and (b) derive, for each such o0o_{0}, a candidate action sequence that will drive the subsequent world-model rollout. To obtain a broad distribution of starting states without costly full episode resets, we adopt a backward-reset randomisation strategy: at the beginning of each trajectory, we roll out the actor for a short reverse-navigation horizon in the game, interleaved with stochastic yaw perturbations, so that every new trajectory starts from a fresh and semantically varied location.

Given o0o_{0}, the corresponding navigation task is not manually specified; instead, we prompt a VLLM (Qwen3.5-27B) with a dedicated two-step instruction-generation prompt—reproduced verbatim below—which first identifies reachable nearby objects in o0o_{0} and then produces a concise, direction-free goal-navigation instruction ℓ\ell anchored on one of them. This adaptive instruction-generation scheme ensures that ℓ\ell stays semantically aligned with the current scene, and that the generated instruction carries the same style as the Goal-Navigation Captions used during Stage I pretraining. The actor then maps (o0,ℓ)(o_{0},\ell) to a candidate action sequence; to broaden the exploration space at rollout time, we use stochastic decoding during actor inference (temperature sampling with T=0.3T{=}0.3 in our default setting), so that the same (o0,ℓ)(o_{0},\ell) can yield mutually distinct candidate sequences. We deliberately use the Stage-I SFT actor, rather than the raw base VLLM, at this step: as noted in Sec. 5.2 of the main text, the SFT actor already possesses a basic embodied-planning ability, so that its sampled sequences contain a non-trivial fraction of correct decisions and—combined with the randomised decoding above—yield rollouts of sufficient quality to form informative preference pairs; starting from the base model would produce rollouts too noisy to support effective preference learning, underscoring the necessity of Stage I. Each candidate action sequence is finally executed in GTA5, and the full per-step screenshots together with the action trace are recorded as the reference input to Step 2.

Step 2: Rollout inside the video world model.

Each (o0,𝐚1:T)(o_{0},\mathbf{a}_{1:T}) tuple from Step 1 is repackaged into the input format expected by LingBot-World-Fast [25], consisting of three components: the raw image o0o_{0}, the actor-planned action sequence 𝐚1:T\mathbf{a}_{1:T}, and a free-form scene-caption prompt—together forming the input to the world model. A subtle but important detail is that, when feeding 𝐚1:T\mathbf{a}_{1:T} to the world model, we further calibrate the execution duration of every individual action so that the displacement/rotation magnitude it produces inside the world model matches the physical magnitude of a unit action in the real GTA5 environment; only under such a magnitude alignment can the world model faithfully serve as a behavioural proxy for GTA5. The world model is then run in batch mode at a fixed ×832480\!\times\!832 resolution with 1313 generated frames per unit action. For every executed step, we additionally save one representative frame from the generated video as the post-step state observation, which will in turn be consumed by the VQA-based reward scoring in Step 3.

Step 3: VQA-based reward and preference-pair construction.

After rollouts are produced, we cast reward modelling as visual question answering [33, 34]. For each rollout, we prompt Qwen3.5-27B (served via vLLM with tensor parallelism) to (i) ground the target object referenced by ℓ\ell on the initial frame o0o_{0}, (ii) overlay the predicted target bounding box as a visual anchor, and (iii) at every step t∈[1,T]t\!\in\![1,T] of the rollout, answer a structured question that evaluates whether the agent is approaching the target in the post-step state frame (saved in Step 2). The two prompts used in this procedure—one for target grounding and one for QA-based scoring—are reproduced verbatim in Tab. D. Each scored step returns a tuple (score,confidence,parse_ok)(\text{score},\text{confidence},\text{parse\_ok}), and is filtered on parse validity. With the per-step QA scores in hand, we can readily construct preference-pair samples for DPO training [77].

Step 4: DPO optimisation.

We post-train the Stage-I actor with DPO using LoRA adapters on the same Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct backbone (r=32r=32). Training uses the sigmoid DPO loss with β=0.1\beta=0.1 and a frozen reference model, AdamW with learning rate 5​e−65\mathrm{e}{-6}, a cosine schedule with 10%10\% warm-up, an effective batch size of 6464 (per-device 1×1\times gradient-accumulation 8×8\times 88 GPUs), and a sequence length of 2,0482{,}048. We train for 22 epochs in bf16 with DeepSpeed ZeRO-2 on 8×8\times NVIDIA H20 GPUs.

Appendix E Limitations

While EmbodiedWorld-200K and the accompanying two-stage training recipe provide a reusable foundation for studying Embodied World Agents, our work still has two limitations.

3D virtual games as proxies for the physical world.

As discussed in Sec. 3.1, we intentionally build EmbodiedWorld-200K from modern 3D open-world games, which provide visually rich environments, physically plausible dynamics, and diverse embodied behaviors under a unified interaction framework. They also constitute one of the few scalable sources of large-scale 3D interactive data accessible at academic cost. Although the resulting corpus spans diverse scenes, viewpoints, art styles, and interaction patterns (Fig. 3 and Fig. A1), these environments remain simulated, designer-authored worlds rather than direct observations of reality. Consequently, factors critical for real-world deployment—such as fine-grained physical interaction, sensor noise, uncontrolled lighting, and long-tail human–object interactions—are only partially captured. Nevertheless, we believe this gap does not diminish the value of EmbodiedWorld-200K as a pretraining resource. Advances in modern simulation engines, including high-fidelity physics and rendering, are steadily narrowing the discrepancy between virtual and real environments. More importantly, many priors learned from EmbodiedWorld-200K—such as scene structure, goal-oriented navigation, and embodied exploration strategies—are largely domain-agnostic. In practice, EmbodiedWorld-200K can serve as a scalable open-world pretraining corpus, followed by lightweight adaptation to downstream physical platforms through real-world finetuning or interactive post-training.

Limited action granularity.

To unify trajectories across more than 150 heterogeneous games, EmbodiedWorld-200K adopts a shared coarse action space consisting of W/A/S/D movement, camera rotation, and a no-op action (N). While sufficient for the embodied navigation and planning tasks studied in this work, this abstraction omits fine-grained interaction primitives such as object manipulation, tool use, UI interaction, combat, and other game-specific controls. As a result, EWAs trained on EmbodiedWorld-200K primarily acquire capabilities in perception, reasoning, and navigation across diverse 3D environments, but do not yet support complex task compositions requiring dexterous manipulation or richer multimodal control.

Appendix F Broader Impact

EmbodiedWorld-200K, together with the accompanying two-stage training recipe, is primarily an infrastructure contribution for studying general-purpose embodied agents in open-world 3D environments. In line with NeurIPS guidance, we reflect on both the positive and the potentially negative societal impact that such a release may bring.

Positive impact.

Open-world embodied-agent research has, until now, been fragmented across isolated robot platforms, proprietary simulators, and closed gameplay pipelines, which significantly raises the entry barrier for academic and non-industrial researchers. By releasing a large-scale dataset of over 200K annotated navigation-planning trajectories that spans 150+ 3D open-world games, together with a unified evaluation split, reproducible baselines, and a concrete two-stage training recipe, we aim to lower this barrier and enable groups without access to industrial-scale data or robot fleets to participate in the study of Embodied World Agents. We also expect the scene diversity, the multi-level annotations, and the domain-invariant open-world priors distilled into our baseline to benefit adjacent areas that rely on general-purpose embodied understanding, including assistive robotics, interactive tutoring systems that ground language in visual 3D worlds, and accessible game AI for single-player experiences.

Potentially negative impact and mitigations.

Because the released baseline is explicitly trained to execute open-world navigation instructions, it could in principle be misused as a component for automated manipulation in online games (e.g., bot-driven farming or cheating in multiplayer titles). To reduce this risk, the released model is trained only on the unified W/A/S/D abstraction rather than on platform-specific low-level controls, is not bundled with any game-specific input-injection interface, and is distributed under a research-use license (see App. A.3 for the annotation protocol and the project page for the license terms). All underlying assets—including the gameplay video source OGameData [60], the pose estimator VIPE [61], and the VLLMs employed for annotation and reward modelling—are credited and used within their original license terms, and no personally identifiable information or human-subject data is involved.
